content: Fetal movement counting is a method used by pregnant women to monitor and quantify the movements of their baby. This practice aims to identify potential fetal compromise early, allowing healthcare providers to intervene in a timely manner to improve pregnancy outcomes. However, it may also lead to unnecessary anxiety or interventions in some cases. The objective of this review was to evaluate the outcomes of pregnancies where fetal movement counting was performed routinely, selectively, or not at all, and to compare different methods of fetal movement counting. The review included five studies involving a total of 71,458 women, with one large cluster-randomized controlled trial (RCT) accounting for 68,654 participants. None of the studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias across all criteria. Most studies included women with uncomplicated pregnancies, except for one that focused on high-risk pregnancies. Key Findings: 1. Routine Fetal Movement Counting vs. Mixed or Undefined Counting: No studies reported on the primary outcome of perinatal death or severe morbidity. In one large cluster-RCT, there was no significant difference in stillbirth rates between groups (low-quality evidence). Caesarean section rates were similar between groups (low-quality evidence). Routine fetal movement counting was associated with a significant reduction in maternal anxiety (moderate-quality evidence). Maternal-fetal attachment did not differ significantly between groups (low-quality evidence). One study found an increase in antenatal admissions after reports of decreased fetal movements (low-quality evidence). Birthweight below the 10th percentile was not significantly different between groups (low-quality evidence). 2. Formal Fetal Movement Counting (Modified Cardiff Method) vs. Hormone Analysis: Caesarean section rates did not differ significantly between groups. Women in the fetal movement counting group had significantly fewer hospital visits compared to those in the hormone analysis group. Apgar scores below seven at five minutes were less frequent in the hormone analysis group. No significant differences were observed in other reported outcomes, and perinatal death or severe morbidity was not reported. 3. Once-a-Day Fetal Movement Counting (Count-to-10) vs. More Frequent Counting (e.g., After Meals): Caesarean section rates were not significantly different between groups. Perinatal death or severe morbidity was not reported. Women were more compliant with the count-to-10 method, as it was less disruptive to daily activities. Limitations: Most studies were small and used different methods, making it challenging to combine results in meta-analyses. The nature of the intervention did not allow for blinding of participants or clinicians. The evidence was often of low quality due to imprecise results and concerns about bias. Conclusions: This review does not provide sufficient evidence to guide clinical practice regarding fetal movement counting. Notably, no trials compared fetal movement counting with no counting at all. Indirect evidence from a large cluster-RCT suggested that routine fetal movement counting might help identify more at-risk babies, but this did not lead to a reduction in perinatal mortality. Further robust research is urgently needed, particularly studies comparing routine fetal movement counting with selective counting, as the latter is often introduced only when fetal compromise is already suspected.
